Great to see another board added to the collection!

As you may already be aware, patch files aren't allowed to be merged (CI checks will reject them), so those will need to be merged into their respective upstream project as appropriate before this can go ahead.

Also, for the sake of easing the review process, it'd be nice to split this up into a series of smaller pieces, e.g. one patch adding the bare-bones build support defining the platform, then follow-on patches configuring the relevant services (e.g. x86-power-control, obmc-console, etc.).

That said, I've given it a quick skim as it stands, with a few comments/suggestions below...

Thanks for your initial review, Zev! For some reason, I haven't received a notification about your review.

> As you may already be aware, patch files aren't allowed to be merged

The patches have been marked with "Upstream-Status: Pending" and will be sent to upstream once I've confirmed that everything works as expected and that it complies with the design policies.

> Also, for the sake of easing the review process, it'd be nice to split this up into a series of smaller pieces, e.g. one patch adding the bare-bones build support defining the platform, then follow-on patches configuring the relevant services (e.g. x86-power-control, obmc-console, etc.).

Great idea! I'll split the commit into several smaller ones but keep them in one relation chain.
The leftovers of debugging and missing upstream of patches will be solved.
The detailed README here is a very nice thing to include!
Thank you!
...though a risk of feature status lists like this is that they tend to go stale over time (I'm not wholly opposed to having it though).
I understand the risk of it, though, it'd still be good to have a brief overview of the most common features.
Acknowledged

(And as a tiny nit, trimming trailing space would be nice.)

Hmm, has ASRock started doing ethernet (redfish?) over USB for host/bmc firmware interactions?  I wasn't aware of them using that arrangement previously, but I may be out of the loop...

Yep... I am not a huge fan of this, but for some reason the boot-up process becomes incredibly slow if the USB gadget isn't available (same for the KCS interface).

I've seen the first use for it for SMBIOS and BIOS settings synchronisation on other platforms like the ALTRAD8UD-1L or the GENOAD12M3-2Q.
Acknowledged
Does this hard-coded MAC address come from anywhere?

If you refer to "F8:C2:49:A6:09:3B", then yes, that was extracted from the original firmware. However, if you refer to the "SUBMAC", then it is generated from the mac address that is located in the EEPROM on address `0x3f80`.

Hmmm...

```
$ grep F8C249 /usr/share/nmap/nmap-mac-prefixes 
F8C249 Ampere Computing
```

Did that MAC come from an x470 or perhaps a different Altra system?  (I could certainly understand a mixup if you've got multiple systems you're experimenting with, though I also wouldn't be terribly shocked if that particular crossing of wires was from the factory firmware either...)

[...after some grepping...]

Oooh, I see -- this is just borrowed from meta-ampere/meta-common/recipes-ampere/network/ampere-usbnet/ampere_usbnet.sh.  Perhaps we could have some discussion with @thu@os.amperecomputing.com, @thang@os.amperecomputing.com, and/or @khangng@os.amperecomputing.com on a way to promote that into some common area to reuse it instead of just duplicating it in meta-asrock?

I would be happy to review and discuss if there is a proposal to bring this service to common code.

Just one concern FYI: currently our usbnet service restarts itself a few times to eventually get an updated MAC address from inventory (which uses `ethaddr`/`eth1addr` u-boot env var set from `phosphor-networkd`, who listens to the inventory from `entity-manager`s, who in turn gets MAC address from FRUs content, which could also be not present and variables are unset, ...). I'm concerned that might be hard to get approved as a common solution, unless there is a way to get the MAC address and create the USB network device more timely.

(Otherwise, extracting only the USB network device creation part of the script seems to not be very exciting IMO. Granted we could get rid of a few lines and config files in our meta folder, but the script and systemd service to restart the USB network device creation remains. I would say duplicating is appropriate in that case)
I went a different path for now and randomly generated 5 octets. Since the MAC is only used on the USB gadget we can use a static address until a decision was made I'd say.
Is there a particular reason we need a platform-specific device-tree for u-boot here?  Most systems can get away with using a generic one, which is kind of nice if that's viable.
Sorry, that was a left-over when I worked on getting the real MAC address in u-boot too. Will clean this up in the next version as the required nvmem-cell support isn't available in v2019.4.

Do you know if the host firmware size is consistent across board variants?  (If so, great, but the variation in BMC flash sizes makes me wonder about the BIOS flash and if we might need some additional logic in the update machinery.)
The host firmware size is consistent. Only the BMC firmware size is different.

I have mixed feelings about this.

At the moment, my implementation uses a `dtsi` file that provides a generic board configuration, with two `dts` files that include the `dtsi` and define the required flash layouts.

I would be in favour of a single device tree targeting a 32M flash layout only. However, due to the current implementation of flash layouts in `meta-phosphor/classes/image_types_phosphor.bbclass` and the way BitBake handles overrides, it is quite complex to generate a 64M NOR image that uses the 32M flash layout and actually boots (i.e. without JFFS2 discard errors on `rofs`, at least that's what I was triggering in my tests).

Supporting this case would require a significant amount of work in the image generation code, which I do not believe is justified for a single system.

In addition, I am concerned that introducing such changes could have unintended side effects or potentially break other systems that rely on the current layout logic.

as discussed in discord [1], I don't know what problems you are having 


if you use a set of partitions that fit within 32MB the fact that the device is 63 should just leave unused space.

however when 64NB layout was added all partition sizes were increased.  
if you exceed a partition siE we try to create a build failure but historically failed to check several places resulting in runtime failure.

To switch partition boundaries you need to write to the surrounding mtd as otherwise the small parts will have gaps and not line up with the new image.
